t: Count Nodes That Are Great Enough
o: A node is great enough if its subtree has ≥ k nodes and at least k nodes in its subtree have strictly smaller values. Since k ≤ 10, we don't need full subtree multisets — only the k smallest values of each subtree. Post-order DFS returns, for each subtree, its size and its up-to-k smallest values; a parent merges its children's lists (each of size ≤ k) plus its own value, sorts, truncates to k. A node qualifies iff size ≥ k and the k-th smallest value in its truncated list is strictly less than node.val. Example 1 (k=2): node 1 sees {1..7}, 6 values below 7 → counts; nodes 2 and 3 similarly qualify; leaves and small subtrees don't. Merging costs O(k log k) per node, giving O(n k log k) overall — efficient for n = 10⁴.
k: With k ≤ 10, keeping only the k smallest values per subtree suffices; merging child lists is cheap.
Post-order DFS returns (top-k values, subtree size); the k-th smallest being < node.val (strictly) decides greatness.

a.n: Approach 1: Post-order DFS Keeping Top-k Smallest Values
a.i: Recursively gather the k smallest values from both children plus the current node's value, sort, truncate to k. Track subtree sizes alongside. Check the great-enough condition at each node using the truncated list.
s: DFS returns (list of up to k smallest values, subtree size).
Merge children lists + own value; sort; truncate to k.
If size ≥ k and list[k-1] < node.val, increment the global count.

c.python:
class Solution:
    def countGreatEnoughNodes(self, root: Optional[TreeNode], k: int) -> int:
        self.k = k
        self.ans = 0
        def dfs(node):
            if not node:
                return [], 0
            lv, ls = dfs(node.left)
            rv, rs = dfs(node.right)
            vals = lv + rv + [node.val]
            vals.sort()
            del vals[k:]
            size = ls + rs + 1
            if size >= k and len(vals) >= k and vals[k-1] < node.val:
                self.ans += 1
            return vals, size
        dfs(root)
        return self.ans

a.t: O(n · k log k) — each node merges/sorts lists of size ≤ 2k+1
a.sp: O(n + k) — recursion stack plus per-node lists

a.n: Approach 2: DFS with Size Pruning (Early Exit)
a.i: Same idea, but skip descending into subtrees that cannot influence the answer: if a subtree already has fewer than k nodes it can't make its root great enough, though its values may still matter to ancestors, so pruning applies mainly to the comparison step. Practically, one can also short-circuit merging once k values smaller than node.val are found. Complexity improves in practice though worst case is unchanged.
s: During merge, count values < node.val and stop early once the count reaches k.
Combine with the size check to decide greatness without full sorting when possible.
a.t: O(n · k log k) — same worst case, faster constants via early counting

w: Note strictness: "greater than at least k nodes" means strictly smaller values count, and duplicates of node.val do not (Example 3: root 3 with children 2,2 qualifies since exactly 2 nodes are smaller). Recursion depth on a skewed 10⁴-node tree is fine in most environments but iterative DFS is a safe follow-up answer. Generalization: if k were large, use order-statistics trees or merge-sort-tree techniques.
